topic.title: Continuous and discontinuous variation; genetic and environmental causes
topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: Foundation material worth a few marks inside a larger question: a percentage from a bar chart, the type of variation with a reason, an example, a graph to choose or draw, and a cause. Straightforward marks, but only if the reason and the graph type are stated precisely.
mustMemorise: Continuous variation: any value in a range, such as height or length; displayed on a histogram with the bars touching
Discontinuous variation: a few separate groups, such as tongue rolling or hand dominance; displayed on a bar chart with gaps
Genetic causes: mutation and sexual reproduction
A mutation is a random change in the number of chromosomes or the structure of a gene
Environmental causes: for example, diet affects height
notOnThisSpec: Characteristics controlled by many genes (polygenic inheritance) as a named idea
Types of mutation such as substitution, insertion and deletion, and their effects on proteins
How often mutations are harmful, useful or neutral, as a graded statement
Normal distribution curves fitted to continuous data

mustBeAbleTo: Say whether a characteristic shows continuous or discontinuous variation, and give the reason
Give examples of each: height and length for continuous, tongue rolling and hand dominance for discontinuous
Choose the graph for each type and explain it: a histogram with bars touching, or a bar chart with gaps
Read values from a bar chart or histogram and turn them into a percentage of the class
Name the genetic causes of variation, mutation and sexual reproduction, and define a mutation
Explain an environmental cause, such as diet affecting height, and why most characteristics depend on both
sheet.howExamined: Foundation Tier material, set as short parts inside a larger question: Summer 2019 B2 Foundation Q2, Summer 2021 B2 Foundation Q2, Summer 2022 B2 Foundation Q3, and one mark on the type of variation in Summer 2023 B2 Higher Q8(c). Expect a percentage from a bar chart, a type of variation with a reason, an example of each type, a graph to draw or choose, and a cause of variation, usually one or two marks each.
traps: Starting a percentage without the whole class: in Summer 2019 B2 Foundation Q2 the first step of the scheme was adding both bars to find the class size
Drawing the bar chart carelessly: Summer 2021 B2 Foundation Q2 gave separate marks for plotting both bars correctly, for bars of equal width, and for labelling the y-axis with what was counted
Splitting a class in a ratio: in Summer 2021 B2 Foundation Q2, twice as many of one group means dividing the class into three equal parts, not two
Giving an example of the wrong type: Summer 2021 B2 Foundation Q2 asked for one of each, and blood group or hand dominance cannot stand in for height
Matching characteristics to graphs by habit: in Summer 2022 B2 Foundation Q3 each characteristic had to be matched to the graph that suits its data
Working a percentage the wrong way round: Summer 2025 B2 Foundation Q3 found some candidates dividing where they should have multiplied, and a part of a class can never come out above 100%
Drawing a bar graph where the data needed a continuous scale, as some candidates did in Summer 2023 Unit 7 Chemistry Q3

items.stem: Before we start, three things from earlier work. Nobody expects you to know this lesson yet. What is a gene?

options.text: a section of DNA that codes for one protein
options.feedback: A section of DNA that codes for one protein.
A chromosome carries many genes along its length.
That is part of your phenotype. The gene is the code behind it.

options.text: all the DNA in a cell
options.feedback: That is the genome.
Its characteristics: what it looks like and how it works. Variation is differences in phenotype.

options.text: the pair of alleles it carries
options.feedback: That is its genotype. The phenotype is what those alleles, and the environment, produce.
That is its genome.

options.text: the type of cell division that makes its gametes
options.feedback: That is meiosis.

items.stem: On which kind of graph do the bars touch?
items.skill: Recall the difference between a bar chart and a histogram (Mathematics)

options.feedback: A histogram. Its bars sit on a continuous number line, so they touch.
A bar chart's bars stand apart, one for each separate category.
A pie chart has no bars.
A line graph has points joined by a line, not bars.

items.stem: Which of these is an example of continuous variation?

options.feedback: Hand span is measured and can take any value in a range.
Blood group falls into four separate groups: discontinuous.
You can or you cannot: two separate groups, so discontinuous.
Left or right: separate groups, so discontinuous.

items.stem: Which graph should display the body masses of 30 pupils?
items.skill: Choose the graph for measured data

options.text: a histogram, with the bars touching
options.feedback: Body mass is continuous, so the bars touch: no mass falls between two classes.

options.text: a bar chart, with gaps between the bars
options.feedback: Gaps say there is nothing in between, but every mass in between is possible.
A pie chart shows shares of a whole, not how a measurement is spread.

options.text: a line graph joining each pupil's mass
options.feedback: The pupils are not in any order, so a line joining them means nothing. Group the masses into classes and draw a histogram.

items.stem: Which two things give variation a genetic basis?
items.skill: Name the genetic causes of variation

options.feedback: Mutation makes something new; sexual reproduction makes new combinations of what the parents have.
Those are environmental causes.
Mutation is genetic, but diet is environmental.
Sexual reproduction is genetic, but sunlight is part of the environment.

options.text: a random change in the number of chromosomes or the structure of a gene
options.feedback: A random change in the number of chromosomes or the structure of a gene.

options.text: a change caused by the environment, such as a scar
options.feedback: A scar is environmental and is not in the genes at all.

options.text: a change that always harms the organism
options.feedback: Most mutations have no noticeable effect; very few are harmful or useful.

options.text: a skill learned during an organism's life
options.feedback: A learned skill is not in the genes and is not passed on.

findTheMistake.stem: Ruth reads a bar chart showing 28 right-handed and 4 left-handed pupils. She is asked for the percentage of the class who are left-handed. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 is right. Line 2 turns the fraction upside down: it divides the class by the group. The group goes on top and the whole class on the bottom, which gives 12.5%.

prompts.prompt: What is continuous variation, and which graph displays it?
prompts.answer: A characteristic that can take any value in a range, such as height. It is displayed on a histogram, with the bars touching.

prompts.prompt: What is discontinuous variation, and which graph displays it?
prompts.answer: A characteristic that falls into a few separate groups, such as tongue rolling. It is displayed on a bar chart, with gaps between the bars.

prompts.prompt: Why do the bars of a histogram touch but the bars of a bar chart do not?
prompts.answer: A histogram shows measured data: every value in between is possible, so one class runs into the next. A bar chart shows separate groups with nothing in between.

prompts.answer: A random change in the number of chromosomes or in the structure of a gene.

prompts.prompt: Two cuttings from one plant grow to different heights. Why must the cause be environmental?
prompts.answer: Cuttings from one plant have the same genes, so any difference between them comes from the environment, such as water or light.
